s0383: Use the wind direction, precipitation, and temperature data in a diagram to reason about which natural zone forms on each slope of a mountain
s0384: First find which slope gets the precipitation (the side facing the moist wind), then compare the temperatures: a tropical rainforest forms in a hot, wet place, and a desert forms in a hot, dry place.
s0385:
The diagram shows the direction of a moist wind blowing from the sea, the clouds, the precipitation, and the average air temperature at four places on the two slopes of a mountain.
Which place is most likely to have a tropical rainforest (jungle)?
s0393: Moist wind from the left → clouds and rain on the left slope
s0394: The wind blows from the sea on the left; the air rises along the mountainside, cools, and brings rain to the left slope.
s0395: Right slope — dry (the air has lost its moisture)
s0396: The air that crosses the mountain has already lost its moisture, so the right slope is dry.
s0398: The places on the wet slope are 1 and 3; place 1 is high up and cool, while place 3 is at the foot and hot.
s0400: A tropical rainforest needs both warmth and a lot of rain — that is place 3.
s0402: A student who chose A looked only at the precipitation, but place 1 is high and cool (13 °C) — too cold for a tropical rainforest.
s0403: A student who chose B picked the hottest place, but place 2 is on the dry slope facing away from the wind — it is likely to be a desert.
s0404: A student who chose D read the wind direction backwards; place 4 is on the dry slope and is cool.
s0405: First find which slope gets the rain, then compare the temperatures.
s0406:
The diagram shows the direction of a moist wind blowing from the sea, the clouds, the precipitation, and the average summer air temperature at four places on the two slopes of a mountain.
Which place is most likely to be a desert?
s0407: Moist wind from the right → rain on the right slope
s0408: This time the moist wind blows from the right, and the clouds and rain are on the right slope of the mountain.
s0410: The air that crosses the mountain and descends the left slope is dry.
s0412: The places on the dry slope are 1 and 2: place 1 is high up and cooler, while place 2 is at the foot and very hot.
s0413: Desert = hot + very little precipitation → place 2
s0414: A desert forms where it is hot and there is very little precipitation — that is place 2.
s0416: A student who chose A correctly found the dry slope but did not take into account that place 1 is high up and cool.
s0417: A student who chose C chose a wet place under the clouds — there is a lot of precipitation there, so it cannot be a desert.
s0418: A student who chose D looked only for a hot place, but place 4 is at the foot of the wet slope — there is a lot of precipitation there.
s0419: Recall the two conditions a desert needs and find the slope where it does not rain.
s0420: Know specific negative and positive effects of a volcanic eruption on the environment (air, soil, plant and animal life)
s0421: Recall what comes out during a volcanic eruption — lava, ash, and gases (water vapor, carbon dioxide, sulfur gases) — and work out how each of them affects the air, the soil, and living things.
s0422: Which of the following correctly describes an effect of a volcanic eruption on the environment?
s0423: Volcanic gases are made mostly of pure oxygen and clean the air.
s0424: Volcanic ash stays only inside the crater and does not spread to the surrounding area.
s0425: Ash and sulfur gases released into the atmosphere pollute the air and cause acid rain.
s0426: Where lava has flowed, the soil stays dead forever and plants never grow there again.
s0427: A volcano releases: lava, ash, gases
s0428: When a volcano erupts, lava, ash, and various gases come out.
s0430: Most of the gases are water vapor, carbon dioxide, and sulfur gases, not oxygen.
s0432: Sulfur gases combine with moisture in the air to form acid rain, and the ash pollutes the air.
s0433: Wind carries ash hundreds of km; lava weathers and over time gives fertile soil
s0434: Wind carries ash very far, and over time lava weathers and turns into fertile soil — so B and D are wrong.
s0436: A student who chose A did not know what volcanic gases are made of; they contain almost no oxygen and instead contain poisonous gases.
s0437: A student who chose B thought ash is heavy and stays where it falls; fine ash is carried very far by the wind.
s0438: A student who chose D thought short-term damage is permanent; over time lava weathers and plants grow there again.
s0439: Recall which gases come out of a volcano and what they form with water in the air.
s0440: Despite the danger, many farmers live and farm at the foot of extinct volcanoes or volcanoes that erupt from time to time. What is the main reason for this?
s0441: The soil formed from volcanic ash and weathered lava is rich in minerals and fertile.
s0442: Near a volcano the air is always cool and it rains a lot.
s0443: The heat of the lava protects crops from frost in winter.
s0444: Insect pests do not live near volcanoes at all.
s0445: Volcanic ash and lava — rich in minerals
s0446: Volcanic ash and lava are rich in elements that plants need, such as potassium, phosphorus, and magnesium.
s0448: When they weather over time, they form very fertile soil.
s0450: That is why large harvests are grown at the foot of volcanoes, and people live there despite the danger.
s0451: This is a positive effect of a volcano on the environment
s0452: This is a positive, long-term effect of a volcanic eruption on the environment.
s0453: Answer: A) the soil is fertile
s0454: A student who chose B thought the climate near a volcano is always cool and wet; climate depends on the region, not on the volcano.
s0455: A student who chose C imagined that lava is always flowing and warming the surroundings; between eruptions the lava cools and hardens.
s0456: A student who chose D made an unfounded generalization; insects live at the foot of volcanoes as usual.
s0457: Think about how the makeup of the soil changes when volcanic ash and lava weather.
s0458: Know that organic waste (from living things) breaks down quickly through the action of microorganisms, while metal, glass, and plastic break down very slowly
s0459: Decide whether the waste comes from a living thing (a plant or an animal) or is an artificial/mineral material: bacteria and fungi break down organic substances quickly.
s0460: The following items were buried in a landfill. Which of them breaks down (rots) the fastest?
s0466: Bacteria and fungi in the soil break down organic substances.
s0467: Apple peel — organic matter from a plant
s0468: Apple peel comes from a plant, and it rots within a few weeks.
s0469: Aluminum, plastic, glass — tens to hundreds of years
s0470: An aluminum can, a plastic bag, and glass are hardly broken down by microorganisms at all; they last for decades or even hundreds of years.
s0472: A student who chose A thought thin metal wears away quickly; aluminum does not rust and lasts a very long time.
s0473: A student who chose C wrongly thought that something light and thin rots quickly; plastic does not break down for hundreds of years.
s0474: A student who chose D thought glass breaks down quickly because it is brittle; even when broken, pieces of glass hardly break down in nature.
s0475: Think about which waste bacteria and fungi can break down as “food.”
s0476: Which of the following items lasts the LONGEST in nature without breaking down?
s0482: A newspaper is made from wood, cotton fabric from cotton fiber, and a banana peel comes from a plant — these are organic materials.
s0483: Banana peel — weeks; newspaper — months; cotton fabric — months
s0484: A banana peel breaks down in a few weeks, and a newspaper and cotton fabric in a few months.
s0485: Glass — a mineral material, microbes do not break it down
s0486: Glass is a mineral material made from sand; microorganisms cannot break it down, and it lasts for thousands of years.
s0488: A student who chose A thought paper is an artificial material; paper is made from wood fiber and breaks down fairly quickly.
s0489: A student who chose B thought fabric lasts a long time because it is strong; cotton is a natural fiber and it rots.
s0490: A student who chose C did not notice the word “longest” in the question and chose the item that breaks down fastest.
s0491: Find the item that does not come from a living thing.
s0492: Know that when the temperature of a substance changes, the speed of its molecules changes (temperature is a measure of the average speed of the molecules)
s0493: Recall that molecules move faster when the temperature rises and slower when it falls; heating or cooling does not change the size, mass, or number of molecules.
s0494: A closed plastic bottle of air was put in a freezer, and the temperature of the air dropped. What happens to the air molecules in the bottle?
s0499: Temperature — a measure of molecular motion
s0500: The temperature of a substance shows how fast its molecules are moving.
s0502: When the air cools, the molecules start moving more slowly.
s0503: Size and number do not change
s0504: The molecules themselves do not get smaller, and because the bottle is closed, their number does not change either.
s0505: Answer: A) they move more slowly
s0506: A student who chose B took the contraction of an object in the cold to mean that the molecules get smaller; in fact, the distance between the molecules decreases.
s0507: A student who chose C thought the air “decreases” in the cold; in a closed bottle the number of molecules does not change.
s0508: A student who chose D got the relationship between temperature and molecular speed backwards.
s0509: Recall how the speed of molecules changes when the temperature drops.
s0510: The water in a kettle was heated, and its temperature rose. Which property of the water molecules increases?
s0513: the average speed of the molecules
s0515: Heating → energy is given to the molecules
s0516: When we heat water, we give energy to its molecules.
s0518: Thanks to this energy, the molecules move faster on average, and that is why the temperature rises.
s0519: Size, number, mass — do not change
s0520: The molecules do not get bigger, their mass does not change, and heating does not increase their number.
s0522: A student who chose A took the expansion of a heated object to mean that the molecules get bigger; in fact, the distance between the molecules increases.
s0523: A student who chose B thought heating creates new molecules.
s0524: A student who chose D wrongly thought a molecule that gains energy gets heavier; the mass of a molecule does not change when it is heated.
s0525: Recall that sugar or tea spreads faster in hot water, and think about how this is connected with the motion of molecules.
